bank.title: Opening a bank account
steps: Choose a bank; book an appointment online or walk in. Many banks also open accounts in the app.
Staff check identity and address, then ask about your status (student / worker) and why you want the account.
Student accounts usually need proof of study; worker accounts usually need proof of employment.
Card and PIN arrive by post to your UK address in about 5-7 working days.
bring: University enrolment letter or employment contract
Proof of UK address if you have one (tenancy agreement, university accommodation letter)
pitfalls: Proof of address is the most common blocker; ask whether a university or accommodation letter is accepted.
Some banks only accept a letter sent to your UK address, so ask about the exact rules.
Digital banks can be an alternative if a high-street bank refuses.

gp.title: Registering with a GP (doctor)
steps: Find a nearby surgery on the NHS website (nhs.uk, 'Find a GP').
Ask at reception or online for the new patient registration form (often called GMS1 or a local form).
Fill it in; you will be asked for name, address, date of birth and any medical history.
You may be invited for a short new-patient check. Registration is free.
bring: Passport or other ID if you have it
Your address and a phone number
List of medicines you take, if any
pitfalls: Surgeries should not refuse registration only because you lack ID or proof of address.
For emergencies call 999; for urgent non-emergencies call 111.
Register early, before you are ill.

landlord.title: Renting a home
steps: Search on listing sites and book viewings. Ask about total monthly cost, including bills and council tax.
The agent or landlord runs referencing: ID, right to rent check, income or student status, and often a UK guarantor.
Read the tenancy agreement before signing; ask what the deposit is protected under.
Pay the deposit (max 5 weeks' rent for most tenancies in England) and holding deposit; get receipts.
bring: Visa or eVisa share code for the right to rent check
Proof of income, funding or student status
pitfalls: Never pay a deposit or rent before a viewing and a written agreement.
Ask for the deposit protection scheme certificate within 30 days.
International students without a UK guarantor may be asked for rent upfront; ask what alternatives exist.

shopping.title: Shopping and everyday payments
steps: Most shops take contactless card or phone payments (usually up to 100 pounds without a PIN). Cash is accepted but less common.
In supermarkets you can use a self-checkout or a staffed till. Ask a member of staff if the machine shows an error.
Shops may ask if you want a bag; there is a small charge for carrier bags (about 5-10p depending on the nation).
Keep your receipt. You need it for returns, refunds and faulty goods.
bring: A contactless debit card or phone wallet
Photo ID if buying alcohol or other age-restricted items (many shops ask anyone who looks under 25)
Receipt for anything you may return
pitfalls: Prices on shelves already include VAT, so there is no extra tax at the till.
Loyalty cards (e.g. Clubcard, Nectar) are optional and free; you do not need one to shop.
If an item is faulty you usually have 30 days to reject it for a refund. For online orders you can generally cancel within 14 days.
Large shops in England and Wales usually open for a shorter time on Sundays, often about 6 hours.

visa.title: Immigration status and visas
steps: Use only official GOV.UK pages for visa applications, status checks and updates. Search 'GOV.UK visas and immigration'.
Most people now prove their status online with an eVisa. Use 'View and prove your immigration status' on GOV.UK to see your status or create a share code.
Landlords and employers may ask for a share code. You create it yourself on GOV.UK; it is free and lasts a limited time.
Keep your passport, application reference and any Home Office emails safe, and check your details are correct.
bring: Application reference or Home Office email
Your UKVI account details (email and phone used to apply)
Any letters from the Home Office
pitfalls: Never pay a third party to get a share code or log in to your account; GOV.UK does not charge for this.
Beware of scam calls, texts or emails claiming to be the Home Office and asking for payment.
Rules and fees change often. Always check the current GOV.UK page and your own decision letter.
For complex cases, refusals or deadlines, get free or regulated advice (e.g. a university advice service, Citizens Advice, or an OISC-registered adviser). This tool cannot give legal advice.
